x.name: Aaron Levie
x.bio: ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI

tweets.text:
Agent swarms have the potential to drive yet another leap in output from AI. The impact will be a clear separation between teams that adopt this pattern of work and those that don’t. 

The progression has roughly been: chat gave us quick turn AI responses that let us work a bit faster, but we were still rate limited by our interactions; then agents that can go off and complete entire tasks for us, accelerating hours or days of work into minutes; to now swarms of agents that are goal seeking and will find any route to the successful completion of a project, where there’s no inherent limit to the productivity gains. 

We can imagine a future where, for any task in which value can be created within a self-contained digital environment, swarms will be able to complete the work faster than any other approach.

Essentially any area where value creation is currently bound by the amount of research you can do, the amount of decisions made with a set of software tools, the amount of data processed or consumed, and the amount of code (or code adjacent) that can be generated. 

This means swarms will play a big role in game development, coding, trading, life sciences research, IT automation, cyber, math breakthroughs, animation, and plenty of other areas of work that have these characteristics. 

There’s a lot of opportunity to build the harnesses, applied AI products, and infrastructure for how these agents operate. And most importantly there’s a ton of opportunity for those that can wire up work in this way. It’s going to be an entire new field of FDE work available.

Agents are going to work with enterprise files 100X more than people do today. This is why we're excited to partner with Anthropic to bring full read/write interoperability to Box content via Claude.

Now you can have an agent not only pull up content to work with in a workflow, but also write back file updates to Box and view them directly inside of Claude, all via MCP. You can create, edit, and update contracts, presentations, strategy docs, and any other content.

When we started Box we couldn't have imagined all the ways that we'd be working with our unstructured data in the future, but it's clear that agents and people will be producing vastly more artifacts than we imagined. We're building the platform that makes it incredibly seamless and secure to work with your content from any agent.

tweets.text: @Google @every Read the full vibe check: https://t.co/UQseDcXkqh

BREAKING:

@Google just dropped Gemini 4 Carbon. It’s a much better coder than Argon—but I’m probably keeping Argon for writing.

We’ve been testing it at @every across coding, writing, design, and knowledge work. It can work for hours on an ambitious project, but it doesn’t always know when to stop.

Here’s your day-zero vibe check:

• Coding: On one run of our Senior Engineer benchmark, Carbon scored 44%, versus Argon’s 21%. A big improvement, though still middle of the pack. In a separate test, @hammer_mt gave it a backlog to work through. It identified 6 tasks as ready, then did 15—including work someone else was already doing. He stopped it after almost 4.5 hours.

• Big builds: @RandyCounsman gave it 3D scans of our podcast studio and an equipment list. In one attempt, it built a browser-based model accurate enough to check whether new gear would fit without getting into the shot. He estimates Carbon also wrote about 95% of a big update to Everycut, our internal video editor.

• Code quality: @kieranklaassen values its tests and documentation on large projects, including its record of approaches it considered and rejected. Fable remains his first choice, but Carbon has earned a place alongside it. The catch: It can produce huge files where Fable keeps things more modular.

• Audio and video: Randy found it caught audio editing issues other models missed. Kieran handed it a recorded meeting and asked for shorts. It came back with 6 titled clips.

• Design: @jackcheng got a hyperrealistic ginkgo-leaf app icon with details other models struggle with. Objects and 3D scenes look better than Argon’s. Interfaces split the team: Jack and Randy kept getting boxes within boxes, while @TylerNishida liked its ideas for new interfaces. Kieran says giving it design guidance makes a big difference.

• Writing: Our editorial benchmark put Carbon and Argon about even. If you like Argon, you’ll probably like Carbon. But Carbon costs more, and I haven’t seen enough improvement to justify switching.

My Reach Test: 🟨 I’ll use it sometimes.

Give it one big job with a clear finish line, and review what comes back. It’s also worth trying as a second opinion, especially on audio and video.

Full vibe check coming soon: https://t.co/Ch2pNl9Po5

Like, that's something that I feel like every generation, that-that's why I was so interested to build this thing in the first place. Yeah. Like, every generation, you have those tools that define that moment, right?

And, and so to me it was like, yeah, there's room for a new generation, and this new generation is not gonna be distributed in the same places that it was before.

So since the beginning I was, like, very focused on, okay, we, we gotta be number one when someone asks about that. Yeah. You're very number one, CloudCode recommending 60% plus of the time.

I think it'll be fun to see the playbook, how do you, how do you win that? Um, I do wanna get back into, okay, so you said you had no idea why email, how to start email. Yeah.

I think a lot of people actually don't understand what goes into making a service like this, right? Yeah. Uh, you might 'cause you've set it up.

Some people would just, you know, "Okay, I can use Twilio, I can use SendGrid, I can use you guys." Yeah. But what goes into making a tool to just mass send emails? What do people not think about? Yeah.

There's just a lot of different things you can do because landing on the inbox, especially when you're doing high volume, is different from, like, when you're scaling just, like, an, a-an app where you throw GPU at the problem, or you just scale more vertically or horizontally, whatever it is.

With email, you gotta respect the rules of the game, and how Gmail behaves is differently from Outlook and differently from Yahoo Mail, and it's an industry that is fascinating because it's so old school and it relies a lot on, on contacts.

But what we found early on was like, okay, we ha- we knew nothing about this world, and so, and, and coming from this perspective, like extremely naive, was the best thing that ever happened.

Uh, like, honestly, like, it was the best thing because, like, there's no preconception of what is right, what is wrong.

So for them, for example, every single app, you go and then first thing you see is, like, this form that you gotta fill out about, like, how many emails we're gonna send, what's the volume, what are you trying to do?

And then you go through a human verification process. Two days later they accept you or, or deny you. Most of the times they're gonna deny you. And I was like, "This doesn't make any sense," right?

[chuckles] Like, why are we blocking people? So I know I'm gonna remove that friction completely, and the friction will be on us. We're gonna figure that out.

Of course, now four years, three years in, in-into this business, I get it why they do that. [laughs] There's just so much fraud and phishing and abuse across the board.

I don't talk too much publicly about that, but we build, like, all sorts of crazy systems internally for that.

But to your question, like, how you architect that, like for example, when you're sending an email to 100,000 people, if you just throw 100,000 emails, uh, like, to Gmail, what Gmail will do is they're gonna throttle the emails because it's way too much, and they, they wanna see the engagement.

So what you do is, like, they see, like, okay, are people opening the emails? Are people archiving, deleting right away or, or not interacting?

Okay, depending on those initial, uh, interactions, then what I'm gonna do with the rest of the emails will dictate that, that beginning.

So there are clever things you can do where 100,000 people put the most engaged audience members in the beginning of that queue. You have to put that in a queue.

You, you need to-- It's an art and a science where you gotta space out each batch. [chuckles] So, and space out between the different providers too, and yeah, now we're, like, buying different IP blocks.

You gotta look at the history of the IP blocks, distributed folks into different IP pools, and then balance the IP pools over time. So it's a whole crazy infrastructure game.

How automated can that be or is there a lot of human judgment still? Yeah. It's a lot of automation, for sure. Yeah. Uh, and I think over time we learned that, okay, this is how fast we can send for new customers.

Of course, if you're sending more, then maybe you can send faster, but there's a, a, a throttle that we have to do to protect you as a sender.

So, like, what Gmail and all these players will wanna see is, like, a graph that is consistently sending more and more, versus what most people do, which is, like, you send once to a big audience, and then you never send again.

And then it's empty, and then boom, uh, you send it again. One, uh, once a week? Twice a week? Yeah. And those are patterns that an abuser will have, right? Mm.

So the whole way of thinking about email marketing and, and email in general is you, you need to do exactly what an abuser wouldn't do. It's the opposite of that. So what, what's a, a abuser do? They buy a domain.

We have now... Like, there was a Japanese gang that recently came. They, they brought, like, maybe 20,000 domains at recent.

Like, those are 20,000 different TLDs registered in different domain registrars, and we look for every single factor there. So they, they come in, it's a domain that was bought two days ago, so- Mm...

very new domains, they, they get bad reputation. Then you, you look at the website, is it returning 200 or basic things like that. Some people don't even set that up or they do, like, a lookalike domain.

So they're like, "Oh, maybe I'll do another domain for code outreach." That's terrible because it's, it looks like you're phishing, right? Like, because you're, you're using a domain that looks, like, the same.

So all these little things, and they just do s- they send a lot of emails all at once, and then they never send again.

So you kinda gotta reverse engineer how phishing works and, and build a platform [chuckles] that does exactly opposite of that. Do you have a list somewhere, or do you recommend people go to some well-known lists?

Yeah, what I've learned is, again, another thing I didn't know, email is the type of world where it requires a lot of education, but people are not interested in learning, right?

Like, the platform should do all those things for them. So we added, like, insights inside the product, so people can just apply the insights.

So we look at sending patterns, and now with AI, it's pretty cool too, like we have link checkers and spell checkers, like all these checkers in, uh, before you send.

So yeah, it's a mix of you're teaching your audience, but at the same time, the product needs to do the teaching. And the more you can bake in the, the best practices, the better.

So one example too, when you send an email, you can send an HTML version and a plain text version. Very early on, we were like, "You know what? Like this-- The whole world is changing.

There are way more agents than, than before. Let's just generate, auto-generate the, the plain text version, uh, of each email." We can extract from the HTML, the markdown, and then just send that.

So we start sending that automatically, and that increased deliverability a ton. You know, it's so much easier for spam filters to just look at the content directly without having to parse that.

Uh, so those things that we are like, "Oh, no, let's bake into that product," and most people don't do that, but we're like, "Oh, that... This makes sense." But with plain text, there's no tracking, right?

There's no tracking. 'Cause you can't embed the, the image. That's right. So you don't have open rates. Yeah. How do you know you have deliverability if you don't have open rates?

Yeah, this is very interesting because the, the industry, there are two ways of tracking, right? You have open tracking and click tracking.

Open tracking, what it does, it, it includes a one-by-one GIF, uh, image, a transparent image, and then if that image is loaded, then you detect that as opened.

The problem with that is that all the changes that Apple did recently in terms of, uh, transparency and, and data privacy, like they read the emails before it lands if they're doing the summaries and all those kinds of things.

So like the open rate as a metric, as a whole, isn't really a- as reliable as it used to be because all these spam filters are, are checking that before. So then you rely on click tracking.

Now, click tracking can also be, uh, difficult because you want the URLs to match the sending domain. You also want the images' URLs to match the sending domain. That's another pattern that an abuser will do.

They would host images somewhere else, point links somewhere else, and then they are sending from these domains. Yeah.

I, I feel like I have, uh, used email services that would rewrite, like for the link tracking, right, they would rewrite to their own domain. Yeah. You're saying that's bad.

That's bad because what hap- We did that too at first. Yeah. And then- I thought that's normal. Yeah, but what's bad is when...

and you have a noisy neighbor problem too, where if one of the customers using that click tracking is an abuser and sends a bunch of phishing, that domain might get listed on a blacklist, and then it takes maybe days or weeks to get out of the blacklist.

So that's how I feel about that too. Like, you come in, we trust you by default. Of course, again, a, a naive way of thinking, but you know what?
